ko-ieyo.gloss: is; am; are (polite, after a noun)

ko-gyeseyo.gloss: stay (polite: 안녕히 계세요, "goodbye" to someone staying)

ko-gayo.gloss: to go (polite: 안녕히 가세요, "goodbye" to someone leaving)

ko-wayo.gloss: to come (polite: 어서 오세요, "welcome"; 왔어요: came; 올게요: I will come)

ko-malhaeyo.gloss: to speak; to say (polite: 말해 주세요, "please say it")

ko-hago.gloss: and; with (after a noun: 떡볶이하고 김밥, tteokbokki and gimbap)

ko-sipeoyo.gloss: to want to (after a verb's -고: 먹고 싶어요, I want to eat)

ko-ui.gloss: 's; of (after a noun: 할아버지의 신문, Grandpa's newspaper)

ko-jjeum.gloss: about; around (after an amount: 삼천 원쯤, about three thousand won)

ko-anieyo.gloss: is not; am not (after a noun with 이/가)

# Usage notes Grandpa Park explains (languages/ko/notes.json). note-<id>-title and note-<id>.

note-yo-title = Ending in 요
note-yo = Polite Korean sentences end in 요 (yo): 알아요, "I know"; 몰라요, "I don't know". To strangers, shopkeepers and your landlady, keep the 요. Drop it only with close friends. The same verb asks or answers: 알아요? "Do you know?", 알아요. "I know."

note-ieyo-title = 이에요 and 예요
note-ieyo = "Is" after a noun is 이에요 when the noun ends in a consonant (책이에요, "it's a book") and 예요 after a vowel (가게예요, "it's a shop"). Introducing yourself, 입니다 works after anything: 저는 …입니다, "I am …".

note-numbers-title = Two sets of numbers
note-numbers = Korean counts things with its own numbers: 하나, 둘, 셋, 넷, 다섯. Before a counter they shorten: 한 개, 두 개, 세 개, 네 개, "one, two, three, four (things)". Prices, months and money use the other set, borrowed from Chinese: 삼 (three), 사 (four), 오 (five), 천 (thousand), 만 (ten thousand). So 삼천 원 is 3,000 won, and 삼월 is March.

note-neun-i-title = 은/는 and 이/가
note-neun-i = 는 (after a vowel) or 은 (after a consonant) marks what you're talking about: 저는 …, "as for me …". 이 (after a consonant) or 가 (after a vowel) marks the subject, often something new or asked about: 이름이 뭐예요? "What's your name?" When in doubt: 는 for "as for", 이/가 for the question.

note-past-title = The past: 왔어요, 냈어요
note-past = Change the 요 ending to 았어요 or 었어요 and it has already happened: 와요, "comes", becomes 왔어요, "came"; 내요, "pays", becomes 냈어요, "paid"; 빌려요, "borrows", becomes 빌렸어요, "borrowed". Put 안 before the verb for "not": 안 왔어요, "didn't come".

note-eseo-buteo-title = 에서, 부터 and 까지
note-eseo-buteo = 에 says where something is (대학교에 있어요, "it's at the university"). 에서 says where it comes from, or where something is done: 대학교에서 왔어요, "it came from the university". For time, 부터 is "since, from" and 까지 is "until": 삼월부터, "since March"; 삼월까지, "until March".

# How to read Hangul: the Book's Letters tab, one message per step in content/languages/ko/letters.json "guide".
letters-guide-blocks = A block is one syllable: a consonant first, then a vowel (beside it or below it), sometimes a final consonant underneath. Read them in that order. ㄱ + ㅣ + ㅁ is gim: the family name English spells Kim, since ㄱ sounds between g and k.
letters-guide-silent = ㅇ at the start of a block says nothing. Only the vowel is read.
letters-guide-join = Blocks read left to right. Join their readings into one word.
letters-guide-type = Type the readings in Latin letters, as the chart shows them. Digits stay digits. Spaces don't matter.
letters-guide-linking = A final consonant can slide into the next block and change the sound. Either spelling works.
